judgments.why: Y is a long, breathless run of dashes with odd asides (the coach split into two rooms, the trunk left at the toll house, the singers judged against Milder), while X is a neat, generic summary of the card.

Y opens mid-letter and carries details the card never gives (the Brussels illumination, Liège and Aachen, the jab at the priests in Berlin, Schlegel's peacock perch), while X just restates the card and adds a moral about the boys.

X has the ironic voice (the ducat fees at Sanssouci, the 'royal' beasts against the 'rabble', flowers that will not show by lantern light) and runs straight on from earlier pages, while Y is a tidy, padded summary.
X is a clipped, exclamatory fragment ('it keeps going on'), while Y adds a stock philosophical aside about Holland lacking historical spirit and a formulaic sign-off.

Y has the real eye-witness texture (the comparison with Cologne cathedral, small groups forming and changing) and a dateline at the end, while X turns the chairs into a lecture on freedom enacted in the body.

Y starts mid-sentence, jokes that the rooms are dry but he is not, and gives practical forwarding addresses, while X garbles the card, making the dialect the reason for the shirt and turning the planned visit to Lange into a dinner that already happened.
Y has the lively theatre criticism (the comparison with Crelinger, 'how they butcher Shakespeare', the English fury), while X has him signing as 'Wilhelm' and preaching about German inner necessity.
X has a concrete side errand (a copy of the Encyclopedia for Beer) and terse practical plans, while Y pads the refusal with a reflection on dignity and independence.

Y has the political-geographic quip about Luxembourg being neither German nor French and a measured account of his fatigue, while X adds a canned 'individual subject to the universal' line and has him decline the invitation, which the card does not say.

X has the dense, dash-strung travelogue (the slag heap, the moonlit Eger, the uncle and Marie's letter in Prague), while Y misreads the card, having him swim in the spring, and closes with the odd 'Kiss me, if you can'.
Y has the exuberant mock-formal toast ('general salvo, universal long live'), the mother at the table and the fireworks weather, while X is generic and signed 'Wilhelm'.
X has his grudging concession of a day, the 36 hours to Prague and the heartfelt run of longing to be home, while Y is a bland paraphrase with filler.
Y is a terse, candid fragment ('I have had quite enough of Dresden'), while X garbles the time ('Early tomorrow morning I was') and pads with aesthetic theory.
X has the 'flesh and blood struggled with the will' dilemma about leaving on 1 October and the scribbling-while-tired voice, while Y is a flat, generic summary.

Y has the idiosyncratic remark on wretched Bohemian villages and the image of candles gilding his memory of her, while X is datelined Prague even though he has already left it, and adds stock greetings.
X holds the rich, intimate account of Goethe's table and of his son, plus the 'your Odysseus' homecoming plan, while Y is a short generic summary.
Y has concrete critical judgments (new, mediocre wall paintings, old-fashioned French gardens, Neptunes and frogs), while X moralizes and is signed 'Wilhelm'.
Y has the wry portrait of the insignificant Saxon niece, the Swabian proverb and the Blue Star inn, while X is a flat paraphrase with stock closings.
Y has rich unprompted detail (Dutch kitchens, Bentheim, the silent Dutch passengers, Bremen's rained-out patriotism), while X is a compressed generic summary.
Y has specific coach lore (the cabriolet versus the side-chaise, the bench like a sofa he is used to sleeping on), while X invents a dateline and odd lines about wine and cards in Berlin.
Y moves on to detailed recollections the card does not mention (Wallraf's Death of Mary compared with Boisserée's, the lawyer who carries Faust as his Bible), while X is generic filler.

X has vivid particulars (Napoleon's lost throne on the hill, the St. Gudula windows, shopping for Marie, van Ghert's convalescence), while Y is a compressed, generic summary with an invented 1822 dateline.
Y begins mid-thought on a Michelangelo ('where else in Germany') and adds the cheerful, well-dressed children, while X restates the card and appends a lecture on the German spirit.
Y has the playful suspense of the reveal ('as whom? — Mr. Heinrich Beer!'), while X pads with doubtful lines about Beer's opinion and the boys' studies.
